title: Caregiver Burnout: The Signs, and What Really Helps
short_title: Caregiver burnout: the signs, and what helps
description: Caring for Mom or Dad and exhausted all the time? Here are the signs of caregiver burnout, why it happens, and what really helps: respite even a few hours a week, support groups, taking care of your own health, and Medicare GUIDE respite for dementia caregivers who qualify.
end: You don't have to do this alone.

parts.head: Caregiver burnout: the signs, and what helps
parts.sub: If you're exhausted all the time, this one's for you
parts.text: If you're caring for Mom or Dad, and you're exhausted all the time, this one's for you. I'm Samantha with Caring Companions in Springfield. Let's talk about caregiver burnout: the signs, why it happens, and what really helps.

parts.head: It isn't a personal failing
parts.sub: Catching it early makes it easier to fix
parts.text: First, burnout isn't a personal failing. It's what happens when someone gives demanding care for a long time, without enough support. And catching it early is what makes it easier to fix.

parts.head: Exhausted, even after rest
parts.text: Here are the signs. You feel exhausted, even after rest. You're more irritable, or you feel resentment toward the person you're caring for, and then you feel guilty about it.

parts.head: Pulling away, and running on empty
parts.sub: Skipping your own doctor. Never enough.
parts.text: You've pulled away from friends, hobbies, or the things you used to enjoy. You're getting sick more often, or skipping your own doctor visits. And it feels like nothing you do is ever enough.

parts.head: It grows little by little
parts.sub: Nobody ever says, this is now a job
parts.text: Why does it happen? Most family caregivers never planned to do this full time. It grows little by little, and there's never a moment when anyone says, this is now a job. Without a plan for relief, the work just keeps growing.

parts.head: Respite, even a few hours a week
parts.sub: Rest, your own doctor, an afternoon for you
parts.text: What helps most is respite, even a few hours a week. A trained caregiver steps in, so you can rest, see your own doctor, or just have an afternoon to yourself.

parts.head: A break isn't giving up
parts.sub: It helps you keep going longer
parts.text: Taking a break isn't giving up. Outside help usually helps a family caregiver keep going longer, not shorter. Think of respite as part of the care plan, not a last resort.

parts.head: Support groups
parts.sub: In person, or through the Alzheimer's Association
parts.text: Support groups help, too, in person or through the Alzheimer's Association. Being around people who understand makes it feel less lonely.

parts.head: Take care of you
parts.sub: Your own doctor, real meals, sleep, saying yes to help
parts.text: And don't skip your own doctor visits. Eat real meals, protect your sleep, and say yes when someone offers to help.

parts.head: Medicare GUIDE respite
parts.sub: 20 visits a year, 4 hours each, if you qualify
parts.text: Caring for someone with dementia? If your family qualifies, Medicare's GUIDE program can pay for twenty respite visits a year, four hours each.

parts.head: Call or text 988
parts.text: And if you ever feel hopeless, call or text 988, any time, day or night.
You don't have to do this alone. Call us at (417) 234-8494, and let's talk about what relief could look like this week. I'm Samantha with Caring Companions.
